name: Widgi Creek
label: Widgi Creek
about_prose: Living on a golf course five miles from downtown Bend means something different than living on one fifteen or twenty miles out. Widgi Creek sits on SW Century Drive, the road that becomes the Cascade Lakes Scenic Byway and carries traffic toward Mt. Bachelor. Ponderosa pine covers the property on the town side, and the Deschutes River Canyon cuts along its edge on the other. The elevation runs close to 3,900 feet, a few hundred feet above the valley floor where most of Bend sits, which is part of why the pine cover here reads heavier than it does closer to the river downtown.

Golf arrived on this stretch of forest in 1991, one of a wave of Central Oregon courses that opened that year as the region's golf-destination era took hold. The course first went by a different name, Seventh Mountain Golf Village, before it became Widgi Creek Golf Club. Robert Muir Graves routed it. Graves spent close to fifty years designing golf courses across the American West, served a term as president of the American Society of Golf Course Architects in the mid-1970s, and had already built the Big Meadow course at Black Butte Ranch nineteen years earlier, in 1972. He died in Bend in 2003, so Widgi Creek is one of the last courses he saw built close to home.

The course plays to a par 72 across 6,911 yards from the back tees, with a 73.4 rating and a 134 slope, threading tight fairways along the canyon rim. Golf Digest named it among the best new courses of 1995 and has kept it on its Best Places to Play list in most years since. Readers of the Source Weekly have voted it Central Oregon's favorite public course more than 20 times. It has always been a public course. A member's guest and a walk-up player from out of state book the same tee sheet. That openness is also the honest trade-off here. This is not a gated, members-only layout like Broken Top or Pronghorn. Anyone can book a Tuesday afternoon tee time, so the golf-course frontage at Widgi Creek comes without the screened privacy those communities sell.

Housing splits into two products. Single-family lots back onto fairways or the Deschutes National Forest boundary, and the Elkai Woods townhomes front the course directly, putting fairway views outside the window without the same lot-maintenance load as a detached home. The two products do not share one homeowners association. A 2020 Oregon Court of Appeals land-use case names three separate entities tied to the property: the Widgi Creek Homeowners Association, the Elkai Woods Homeowners Association, and the Elkai Woods Fractional Homeowners Association. A buyer comparing a single-family lot to an Elkai Woods unit is comparing two different sets of governing documents, not one.

The location's real payoff is the road itself. Mt. Bachelor sits 22 miles further southwest on the same pavement, and the highway continues past the mountain as the Cascade Lakes Scenic Byway. Redmond Airport runs about 35 minutes north. None of that is unique to Widgi Creek. Every address on Century Drive gets the same access. What Widgi Creek adds is proximity to town, five miles out instead of fifteen or twenty for the resort communities further down the same road. There is one seasonal catch on that corridor. Deschutes County closes the highway every winter west of Mt. Bachelor, between the Dutchman Flat and Deschutes Bridge gates, typically from mid-November into the following spring. Widgi Creek sits well inside that closure line and keeps year-round access. It is the road further out that goes quiet each winter, not this stretch of it.

The clubhouse runs a full-service restaurant and bar with an outdoor deck and a banquet room that holds up to 150, open to the public rather than just members. Pickleball courts operate on site with lessons available through the club, and Operation 36 Golf Academy staffs instruction alongside the club's own teaching professionals. None of that requires owning a home here. It does mean a Widgi Creek address puts a restaurant, a pro shop, and instructors within a short drive rather than across town. That fits a buyer who plays golf or pickleball often enough for the distance to matter, and who would rather look out at an active public course than pay for the privacy of a members-only one. It is a poor fit for a buyer set on a gated community. Bend has those elsewhere, and they are built for exactly that instead.
